blocks.label: READING · THE TINY PUMP IN A BEE STING
blocks.html:
Scientists from Macquarie University in Australia have made an exciting discovery about honey bees. They found out why a bee's stinger keeps putting venom into a person's skin even after it has left the bee's body. Honey bees usually die after stinging a person, because their stinger gets stuck in the skin and tears away from their body. But the stinger doesn't stop working.

The scientists used high-speed cameras to film the tiny stinger, which is only two millimetres long. The video showed that the stinger works like a pump. It has two small parts that move backwards and forwards. These parts push the stinger deeper into the skin and help keep the venom flowing. The lead researcher said the design of the pump was "unique". She hopes her discovery will inspire companies to make tiny pumps that could give medicine to people.

A bee sting can be very painful. Most people have pain, redness and swelling after a sting. However, a sting can be dangerous for people who have allergies. Some people have a serious reaction and go into anaphylactic shock. Their face or throat may swell up, or they may have trouble breathing.

If someone is stung, they should remove the stinger as quickly as possible. This will help to stop more venom from entering their body. The person should also wash the area with soap and water. In addition, it is a good idea to put an ice pack over the sting to help reduce pain and swelling. If the person feels unwell, someone should call emergency services immediately.

blocks.label: EXPLAIN IT IN YOUR OWN WORDS
blocks.html: Answer with two or three full sentences. Then reveal a model answer and compare.

items.q: Why does a bee sting keep hurting after the bee flies away?
items.a: Because the stinger stays in the skin and works like a pump. Two small parts move backwards and forwards, so it keeps pushing venom deeper into the skin.

items.q: How did the scientists find this out?
items.a: They filmed the stinger with high-speed cameras. The stinger is so small and so fast that you can only see how it works in slow motion.

items.q: Why could this discovery be useful?
items.a: Companies could copy the design to make tiny pumps that give medicine to people, maybe without pain.

items.q: What are the normal reactions to a sting? And the dangerous ones?
items.a: Normally, people have pain, redness and swelling. People with allergies can go into anaphylactic shock: their face or throat swells up and they have trouble breathing.

items.q: What should you do if someone is stung?
items.a: First, remove the stinger as quickly as possible. Then wash the area with soap and water and put an ice pack on it. If the person feels unwell, call emergency services immediately.

blocks.label: ROLE-PLAY · THE EMERGENCY CALL
blocks.html: Your friend has just been stung by a bee at a barbecue and is not feeling well. You call emergency services.

roles.name: Caller (Thiago)
roles.card: Your friend Marcos, 34, was stung on the neck 5 minutes ago. His lips are starting to swell up and he says his throat feels strange. You are at a house party, Rua das Flores 120. You don't know if he has allergies. Stay calm and explain everything clearly.

roles.name: Operator (teacher)
roles.card: Ask: the address, what happened, when, where on the body, if he is breathing well, if he has allergies or medicine (an EpiPen). Tell the caller: remove the stinger, keep him sitting up, don't give him food or drink, an ambulance is coming in 10 minutes. Ask him to describe any change.
